title: Civic universities need collective approaches to bring students and long-term residents together
summary: In some residential areas, universities’ civic agendas can ring hollow. Kate Seymour presents a collaborative project which aimed to co-create hope in Fallowfield
full_text:
For decades, Fallowfield has provided a home for new arrivals in Manchester.

An historic connection with the city’s higher education institutions means many newcomers are students. Mention Fallowfield to residents, past and present, and it frequently evokes fond recollections and nostalgic affection. If you have ever lived in Manchester, you may well have stories of your own.

But everything in Fallowfield is not as rosy as such nostalgic sentiments may suggest. Walking around its streets, there are signs everywhere of neglect and disrepair. Landlords seeking to maximise occupancy levels have partitioned rooms and built extensions across gardens and into the roofs and basements of their multi-occupied properties. This has led to over-crowding within the neighbourhood, mounting pressures on resources, and the concreting over of green spaces. The high street overflows with takeaways and vape shops, but many other needs are significantly under-served. The situation is particularly acute in the area known historically as Fallowfield Village, which largely coincides with the postcode district M14 6.

It would be easy to blame students for Fallowfield’s ills. Data shows that the suburb has the densest student population in the city. Some streets have over 85 per cent student residents, with only a handful of owner occupiers remaining. Residents suggest litter, anti-social behaviour and late-night noise are perennial problems, echoing common criticism of other heavily “studentified” areas across the UK.

Yet our Collective Inquiry research project, carried out during 2025 and focusing specifically on the M14 6 area, demonstrates that this demographic imbalance is harming not just permanent residents but also students.

Housing lies at the heart of the problem. While many students have the misfortune of living in sub-standard yet over-priced housing, the knock-on impacts are felt throughout the community. Substantial monetary outflows (to absentee landlords amongst others) reduce the ability and will of others to invest in, and commit to, the neighbourhood.

In recent decades, the number of permanent residents has shrunk dramatically, depriving the area of those who might otherwise perform the often invisible civic work that is vital for a well-functioning neighbourhood. Indeed, after only a year, even students frequently move on. Dense impermanent and transient populations make the neighbourhood a target for criminals, giving rise to frequently repeated safety concerns.

Civic universities and the hyperlocal

The situation in hyperlocal neighbourhoods like Fallowfield is a problem for the growing ambitions of civic universities. Historically, universities were focused on the on-campus lives of their students. But in recent years, promoting student welfare has increasingly entailed actively supporting students to navigate off-campus issues as well, such as cost-of-living pressures, the private housing market, safety concerns, and health, wellbeing and belonging.

Meanwhile, there is increasing demand that universities deliver positive social impact: not only in far-flung corners of the world, but also on their doorstep. The five Manchester-based universities have united behind a recently refreshed civic university agenda, aiming to deliver impact for the city region in four key priority areas: opportunity and prosperity, health and wellbeing, culture, and environment.

They are undoubtedly key anchor institutions in the city, creating thousands of local jobs, delivering significant economic and social impact, and helping make Manchester a highly desirable place to work, study and live. Both Manchester Metropolitan University and the University of Manchester independently contribute more economic value (GVA) to the city region than the city’s two leading football teams combined.

Nevertheless, there remains a persistent gap between high-level civic ambitions and the lived realities of hyperlocal neighbourhoods. Organisations like the United Kingdom Town and Gown Association (UKTGA) have long highlighted the importance of long-term, place-based neighbourhood partnerships that recognise students as residents and citizens within shared local spaces.

Yet too often, civic university activity is still articulated at the scale of city regions, innovation districts or strategic partnerships, without translating into sustained relationships with the communities living alongside campuses and student populations. As a result, the civic agenda can ring hollow in long-suffering areas like Fallowfield, where residents’ prevailing lived experience of university neighbours may be a significant negative impact on their quality of life.

Overcoming fragmentation

The Collective Inquiry was a co-created project based on the principle of researching with rather than on communities. The research team consisted of over thirty participant-researchers including long-term residents, staff and students from two universities, representatives from the local authorities and other partner organisations. From the beginning, permanent residents and students were at its heart. We took a multi-perspectival approach to better understand the challenges facing the M14 6 neighbourhood using a variety of techniques, including a walking methodology, a systems mapping exercise, and follow-up interviews. Whilst the team did not agree on everything, we were able to identify points of convergence to focus on shared goals.

Our report identified long-term fragmentation as a key driver behind the problems faced here. Over many decades, as a result of deliberate policy decisions, governance gaps, and unintentional oversights, Fallowfield has fallen between the cracks.

Institutionally, responsibility for proactively supporting and managing student populations in local neighbourhoods sits uneasily between public authorities and universities. Partnerships are typically focused on symptom management, such as minimising the disruption of the annual student move in/move out.

Politically, the area sits between three wards and two constituencies. Ward-level data reporting can serve to obscure demographic characteristics of areas like M14 6 where boundaries meet. Meanwhile local councillors, who are elected to represent residents of their own ward, have struggled to tackle deeply engrained challenges across ward boundaries. As a result, the approach to M14 6 is all-too-often reactive and piecemeal.

Socially, there is a lack of cohesion across the whole community. There are strong student communities as well as strong, if depleted, communities of permanent residents. Yet these worlds rarely overlap and interactions that occur tend to be negative. Conflict between individuals takes the place of collective contestation of the systemic harms impacting both groups: a dynamic not dissimilar to many other polarised societal contexts.

We want to recognise that many groups and individuals have worked hard over the years to overcome these challenges. For example, residents’ groups undertake the grinding work of monitoring and objecting to planning and licensing applications. Community-led projects, often supported by the council’s local neighbourhood teams, seek to restore pride in the area. Recent examples include new public murals, the volunteer-led restoration of the Shakespearean Garden, and Clifton WEB’s tree-base planting. The small Manchester Student Homes Team, supported by excellent student ambassadors, work hard to support local residents and students attending both centrally located universities. Yet in all cases, resources are tight and volunteer initiatives rely on too few people to be sustainable.

Meanwhile, opportunists – many operating in a poorly regulated for-profit housing market – have taken advantage of gaps in governance to extract large profits from Fallowfield and the students who call it home. This has outwardly reduced a distinct neighbourhood with a rich, diverse heritage to a generic student area, reinforced by long-standing cultural narratives and institutional communications. Far from the “vibrant neighbourhoods” championed by the local authorities, fragmentation has left Fallowfield run-down, neglected, imbalanced and unsustainable.

Co-creating hope

In March this year, we held a roundtable to share the outcomes of the Collective Inquiry and discuss how to implement its recommendations. Hosted in Ladybarn Community Hub, the event brought together over 50 participants representing key actors in M14 6: the universities, local authorities, elected officials, student unions, long-term residents, police, landlords, renters and others. To the best of our knowledge, this was a truly historic gathering: the first time that so many key stakeholders have come together to focus on collectively building a better future for the neighbourhood in the neighbourhood.

[image]

In the spirit of the Collective Inquiry, the roundtable was co-led by permanent residents and students. Side-by-side, speakers argued for a strategic, holistic, inclusive and data-informed approach to the neighbourhood. One resident spoke movingly of the experience of ostracism from a neighbourhood in which her family had lived for three generations. Student representatives shared lived experiences of poor housing, exploitative landlords and the need to be valued and supported as citizens of the city. Both groups proposed constructive and complementary measures to drive up the quality of housing, improve communications and develop a place-identity for the benefit of all those who live, work and study in Fallowfield.

We then welcomed three senior respondents: University of Manchester president Duncan Ivison, Manchester Metropolitan University academic registrar Joe Rennie, and Councillor Gavin White, Executive Member for Housing and Developing. We were delighted with their positive responses and commitments to a new shared partnership approach.

The next step is to create a new taskforce for M14 6, co-chaired by students and residents, which will work to improve data, housing standards, communications and place-making. We anticipate that the taskforce will both address long-standing challenges in this neighbourhood and provide a new collaborative model for managing ever-growing student populations across the city region. It will address GMCA priorities particularly around housing, with the potential to connect to innovations like the Good Landlord Charter, and support the implementation of additional HMO licensing. It is our hope that this work will begin to overcome decades of fragmentation.

As participants left the roundtable, many commented on the hope that they now feel for the neighbourhood’s future. This reaction suggests that initiatives like the Collective Inquiry can help to better ground civic universities in place.

At the hyperlocal level, universities need to not only honestly recognise and collectively address negative impacts, but also allow themselves to be impacted by those with whom they share space. This project shows the power of slow, inclusive, co-created and democratically organised research to connect people around shared concerns and empower diverse communities to develop inclusive solutions. We are profoundly grateful for the time, dedication and (often unpaid) work of everyone who has supported this project. The hope now is that the taskforce will drive forward the changes that Fallowfield urgently needs to become a unified, peaceful and sustainable neighbourhood.

This article was written in collaboration with members of the Collective Inquiry research team, whose contributions significantly shaped its development: Helen Aczel, M14 6 resident, founder and former co-ordinator of the South East Fallowfield Residents Group and coordinator of Clifton WEB; Heather Alberro, Lecturer at the University of Manchester; Joel Dowson, Greater Manchester Student Partnership Manager; Kattie Kincaid, M14 6 resident and project lead for the Shakespearean Garden; Jason Lee, University of Manchester graduate and former chair of the Manchester Student Renters Union; and Rosalyn Marron, Senior Lecturer at Manchester Metropolitan University.

We would also like to thank Cooper Healey, Manager at Manchester Student Homes, for her helpful comments on an earlier draft, and colleagues at Manchester Metropolitan University, the University of Manchester and Manchester City Council for their ongoing support.

title: Students have the right to set-off to university
summary: Jim Dickinson considers whether university fee rules leave students with any meaningful leverage when course delivery is disputed
full_text:
The other day when I was out delivering training for SUs, one of this decade’s perennials came up again.

Student leader discussing their experience of their provider describes how different their course and wider set of services was to that which was advertised to them.

We had an interesting discussion along the lines of “what do you think makes that possible?” Usually that conversation draws out the distinction between chooser and user, or the lack of awareness that students have of their rights, or the faulty power dynamics involved in a sector that retains endless trappings of “you’re lucky to be here” when it’s usually the other way around these days.

But one of the officers – an international PGT as it happens – piped up and said:

It’s because they’ve had your money already.

He might be on to something you know. In its (new and revised) guidance on unfair contract terms, the Competition and Markets Authority says:

One legitimate way for the consumer to obtain compensation from a trader is by exercising the right of set-off. Where a consumer has an arguable claim under a contract against a trader, the law generally allows the consumer to deduct the amount of that claim from anything they have to pay. This helps prevent unnecessary legal proceedings.

It also says:

If the right of set-off is excluded, consumers may have (or believe they have) no choice but to pay in full, even when there is something wrong with what they are buying. To obtain redress, they then have to go to court. The costs, delays, and uncertainties involved may in practice therefore deprive them of their rights.

Well, yes. If your course has been awful and you’re paying in installments, it’s not as if you can withhold a couple of those instalments without risking not getting your qualification – and in many cases, risking being shopped to UKVI.

But more broadly:

Terms are more likely to be unfair where consumers are required to pay in full (or nearly in full) before the business has finished carrying out its side of the contract. For example, this includes where a substantial amount of work is carried out for the consumer after full, or nearly full, payment has been made.

Generally, payment for services falls due after the service has been carried out and an invoice is given, so any term which requires substantial earlier payment may be unfair. For example, the consumer could lose their payment if the trader becomes insolvent before completion of the contract.

Such terms also tend to remove or weaken the trader’s proper incentive to perform work with reasonable care and skill.

Or indeed, to deliver the material offer that was originally made.

One of the other officers chimed in and said:

Is it the same thing as why landlords can’t ask for more than a month’s rent now

During the passage of the Renter’s Rights Act, the government was pretty clear about the underlying problem in housing. Tenants lacked “the bargaining power to effect change”.

Ministers said that defenders of advance rent “seriously downplay the imbalance between landlords and tenants”, because in a contested market the supposed freedom to agree six months’ payment upfront can push people into agreements that stretch their finances to breaking point. When the Act passed, the government boasted that the scales had been tipped against tenants for decades and that it was now levelling the playing field.

Students might reasonably wonder why the same analysis disappears at the university gates. An international applicant doesn’t meaningfully negotiate a demand for £10,000 before a CAS is issued. A current student doesn’t freely agree that every instalment must be paid regardless of an unresolved dispute when refusal can mean withdrawal from the course and loss of visa sponsorship.

The power imbalance is at least as obvious. Yet instead of limiting prepayment or protecting the money, the regulatory answer is still to publish the terms clearly.

Set-off and match

Set-off is not a wild concept. It is the basic idea that when two parties owe each other money under the same contractual relationship, the consumer should not always have to pay the trader in full and then start separate proceedings to get some of it back.

Imagine that you’ve had work done on your house. The final invoice is £5,000, but there is an arguable £1,000 of defective work. The consumer law answer is not necessarily that you can refuse to pay anything. But nor should the builder be able to insist on the whole £5,000, forbid any deduction, and leave you to pursue the £1,000 through the courts afterwards.

You pay what is properly owed. You retain a reasonable amount reflecting the arguable claim. There is then a fair process for resolving the difference.

Universities don’t operate like that. The default is usually that the fee debt and the complaint are separate matters. You pay the fee by the deadline. You can complain about the course through another process. If your complaint is eventually upheld, someone might decide whether a refund or compensation is appropriate.

It is “pay now, complain later” dressed up as administrative tidiness.

That distinction matters. A retrospective complaints system isn’t an adequate substitute for the right to set off an arguable claim. The whole point of set-off is that the consumer retains some leverage while the dispute is unresolved. Making the student surrender all of that leverage and then ask the provider to give some money back transfers the financial risk, the delay and the inconvenience entirely onto the student.

And the university is not just any creditor. It controls the student’s access to teaching, assessment, facilities, results, progression and eventually the award. Where the student is sponsored under the Student visa route, it may also control whether continued non-payment results in withdrawal of sponsorship and reporting to UKVI.

The result is that a student withholding £1,000 over an arguable contractual breach is not taking the same risk as a householder disputing a builder’s invoice. The student may be risking the value of the entire course.

Loan and behold

For most home undergraduates, the issue is slightly stranger because the student never handles the tuition fee money at all.

In the English system, where the full-time undergraduate receives a Tuition Fee Loan, the Student Loans Company pays the fee directly to the provider in three instalments – 25 per cent at the start of term one, another 25 per cent at the start of term two and the remaining 50 per cent at the start of term three. The student becomes cumulatively liable for 25 per cent, 50 per cent and then 100 per cent of the annual loan.

On one level, that looks like the sort of staged payment arrangement the CMA regards as preferable to demanding everything up front. Universities incur costs across the year, and payments are spread across it.

But it is staged payment without student control.

The student can’t contact SLC in December and say that the promised contact hours have not appeared, the advertised specialist modules have been withdrawn, the equipment has never worked and £1,500 should therefore be held back from the next payment.

The university confirms attendance. SLC makes the scheduled payment. The student acquires the corresponding loan liability. The contractual dispute follows a separate track.

Attendance is not satisfaction. Confirmation that a student remains enrolled tells us nothing about whether the provider is performing the contract properly. But in the payment system, continued attendance is effectively treated as the trigger for further money to flow.

There is no student-controlled mechanism equivalent to set-off. The student has to allow the university to receive the money, accept the associated loan liability and then pursue a refund. Even if they ultimately secure one, the process depends on the provider correcting or adjusting the position.

Some of that machinery is statutory rather than invented by universities. Terms which merely reflect mandatory statutory or regulatory arrangements have particular protection under the Consumer Rights Act. A university can’t casually rewrite the SLC payment schedule.

But that doesn’t immunise everything surrounding it. Universities still choose their own terms on when fees are treated as contractually due, what happens when a student disputes a sum, whether complaints affect payment obligations, whether refunds are available and what sanctions can follow.

For SLC-funded students, the question is therefore not just whether the student has a formal legal right of set-off. It is what the functional equivalent is supposed to be when the payment architecture has removed their ability to exercise it.

As it stands, the answer appears to be “make a complaint and hope”.

Pay before you play

The position is more direct for self-funding students.

Some are offered instalment plans. Others – especially international students on one-year PGT courses – may be required to pay large sums before enrolment, with substantial further payments due before much of the course has been delivered. In some cases, the whole annual fee is paid in advance.

The revised CMA guidance is pretty clear on this point. It says a term is more likely to be unfair where consumers are required to pay in full, or nearly in full, before the business has finished carrying out its side of the contract.

It goes further:

Generally, payment for services falls due after the service has been carried out and an invoice is given, so any term which requires substantial earlier payment may be unfair.

The CMA identifies two particular problems. The consumer may lose the payment if the trader becomes insolvent before completing the contract. And taking the money early removes or weakens the trader’s proper incentive to perform with reasonable care and skill.

It would be too simple to conclude that all advance tuition payments are therefore unlawful. Universities make commitments in advance. Staff have to be recruited. Timetables, rooms and placements have to be arranged. A place accepted by one student may not realistically be sold to another halfway through the year – although the idea of “places” or courses being “full” looks like mythology in many providers these days.

The question is whether the payment structure is proportionate to those costs and risks – and whether it leaves the student with an effective remedy when performance is disputed.

The CMA says staged payments are more likely to be fair when they reflect the trader’s spending in carrying out the contract and leave the consumer able to retain an amount reasonably sufficient to exercise an effective right of set-off.

That is not the same as dividing a large annual fee into three arbitrary dates and threatening withdrawal if any one of them is missed. A stage payment is supposed to correspond, at least broadly, to performance or expenditure. It should not merely be an accelerated debt-collection device.

Crucially, the guidance also says that where full payment genuinely has to be made in advance, the money should be held under secure arrangements that protect it if the trader becomes insolvent and prevent its release until a dispute has been resolved.

That sounds more like escrow than an ordinary university (or, I might add, franchise partner’s) bank account.

Universities requiring the whole fee in advance are unlikely to be treating it as money held on behalf of the student pending satisfactory delivery. It is treated as the university’s income. The institution has the benefit of the cash. The student bears the delivery risk and then has to pursue the institution’s own processes if the bargain is not honoured.

Going concern, going, gone

There is an awkward crossover with OfS’s new financial risk categories. Category 4 doesn’t mean that a provider is feeling a bit wobbly. It means acute financial concerns – consistently negative operating cashflow, a short-term risk of running out of cash, and possible reliance on borrowing or third-party support to keep operating. Category 5 means market exit.

At that point, the insolvency risk in the CMA guidance is not exactly hypothetical. How could a provider known by its regulator to be at material risk of closure continue requiring an international student to pay a year’s fees in advance, sweep the money into its general working capital and leave the student as an unsecured creditor if it collapses? Surely the choices are to stop demanding substantial prepayment, collect fees in stages as teaching is delivered, or place the money somewhere genuinely protected.

And “somewhere protected” ought to mean more than a separate account with the university’s name on it. If the money still belongs to the provider and can be reached by its other creditors, it has not really been protected at all. The CMA appears to be contemplating something closer to escrow, a trust, a bond or insurance – arrangements that mean the student’s money survives the provider’s failure.

In England, OfS almost gets there. A student protection direction can require a provider to explain how it will handle complaints, refunds and compensation – including how it will fund them when its finances are already stretched. But that is planning for what happens after the trouble arrives. Protecting future fee payments would stop the provider using the money of students it may never teach to keep itself alive for a few more weeks.

In fact, ring-fencing substantial advance payments looks like an obvious requirement for every provider placed in Category 4. Otherwise the regulator may know that the provider is at material risk of market exit, the provider may know, its lenders may know – but the student is still expected to transfer tens of thousands of pounds into the danger zone.

Ironically, complying with the law (or at least CMA’s revised interpretation of it) would probably push some providers currently in Category 4 into Category 5 (Market Exit) and some in Category 3 into Category 4 (material risk of it).

Oddly, none of this appears in the OfS’s proposed new condition C6 on treating students fairly. The draft would expressly prohibit a university from writing away a student’s right to set off a claim against fees still owed. It would require clear refund and compensation policies, and tell providers to identify risks to delivery and act early. But it says nothing about whether the money needed to pay those refunds should still be there.

In fact, institutional closure is deliberately carved out of C6 and handed over to C4, under which the OfS can require a bespoke Market Exit Plan once it decides that closure presents a material risk. That may eventually involve asking how refunds and compensation will be funded. But there is no automatic requirement to protect the fees being collected in the meantime – no escrow, trust, bond, insurance or ring-fenced account.

So a provider can be in acute financial difficulty, require an international student to pay a year in advance, use that student’s money to maintain operating liquidity and only later be asked how it proposes to fund the refund if the course disappears. That is not really student protection. It is allowing students’ prepayments to finance the period immediately before they need protecting.

A fee by any other name

There is a related issue with international student deposits.

The word “deposit” makes a payment sound small, provisional and attached to the reservation of a place. But some institutions require sums running into several thousand pounds before issuing a CAS or allowing enrolment.

The CMA says a genuine deposit can sometimes be retained if it operates as a binding reservation, is disclosed at the earliest opportunity and has precise, clear and narrow conditions governing when it is non-refundable.

But it also says that such a deposit will not normally amount to more than a small percentage of the total price. A larger prepayment may be a disguised penalty.

Calling half of an annual tuition fee a “deposit” does not make it one. It may simply be a substantial advance payment with restrictive refund conditions.

There may be legitimate reasons to require evidence that an international applicant can fund their studies. There may be costs associated with admissions work, CAS issuance and places that cannot be filled at short notice. But those arguments justify recovering reasonable, evidenced losses. They don’t automatically justify retaining a large payment whenever a student does not enrol, regardless of the circumstances or the university’s actual loss.

Debt to rights

The sector’s existing complaints approach tends to start from the opposite direction.

The OIA says that where providers have published clear information about payment requirements and deadlines, it will usually be reasonable to suspend or terminate the enrolment of a student who does not pay. It also says providers must give students a route to challenge decisions relating to fee payments, and that international student cases should be dealt with promptly so that errors are identified before a visa is curtailed.

That is understandable where the debt is undisputed. Universities have to collect their income. A student can’t just decide that fees are optional, ignore correspondence and continue indefinitely.

But the revised CMA guidance exposes a missing distinction. There is a difference between:

I cannot pay the instalment.

I do not intend to pay the instalment.

And:

I accept that most of the instalment is due, but I have an arguable claim arising from your failure to deliver the contract and am withholding a proportionate amount.

Almost all university debt policies collapse all three into “non-payment”.

The student may be told that complaints do not suspend the obligation to pay. The entire outstanding sum remains due. Debt sanctions continue while the complaint is considered. Any payment made will be allocated against whatever debt the university chooses. No deduction, counterclaim or set-off is permitted.

That is the practical problem the CMA is describing. The student is required to pay the whole amount even when there may be something wrong with what they are buying. The route to redress comes afterwards, carrying costs, delay and uncertainty that may deprive the student of the right in practice.

It becomes still harder to defend where the university can impose the sanction without obtaining a court judgment. The revised guidance specifically identifies concern where a trader can impose a sanction on a consumer without first going to court, because the consumer has not paid the whole price demanded.

A university can therefore decide that the whole fee is due, reject the student’s proposed deduction, classify the sum as debt, terminate registration and rely on the termination to end further delivery. In an international case, the consequences can extend into immigration status.

That is quite a lot of unilateral power arising from a sum that may genuinely be disputed.

Fair pay, fair play

None of this means that writing “set-off” in an email should operate as a magic spell.

A student shouldn’t be able to transform a vague complaint about teaching into an entitlement to withhold the entire fee. A claim would need to be genuine and arguable. The amount retained would need to be proportionate. The student should pay the undisputed balance and engage with a process for resolving the rest.

But the university would have obligations too.

Its terms should distinguish disputed sums from ordinary arrears. It shouldn’t suspend or withdraw a student solely over a reasonably quantified, bona fide disputed amount while an expedited process is operating. It shouldn’t demand payment of the whole sum as the price of accessing that process.

There should be a rapid initial decision on whether the claim is arguable. That isn’t the same as deciding the whole complaint. It’s a triage stage capable of filtering out fanciful claims while protecting students who have raised a serious issue.

For large or consequential disputes, there should be independent adjudication. A university marking its own contractual homework while holding both the money and the power to terminate the consumer is not a balanced dispute-resolution system. It’s not clear that the OIA would, at present, count – and anyway, consumer law applies UK-wide.

Self-funding students could be allowed to pay the disputed amount into a protected account. SLC-funded students need a mechanism through which a successful complaint can produce a prompt adjustment to the fee and associated loan liability – not just a discretionary payment several months later.

And universities reviewing their terms should be searching for familiar formulations:

All fees must be paid without deduction, counterclaim or set-off.

The submission of a complaint does not affect your obligation to pay.

Any failure to pay any amount by the deadline may result in suspension or withdrawal.

Those clauses may have felt like standard debt-management boilerplate. Read alongside the revised CMA guidance, their effect looks a lot more significant.

A rights issue

The CMA’s higher education guidance has spent more than a decade telling universities that students are consumers. The sector has responded by producing longer terms and conditions, larger pre-contract information sets and more elaborate complaints procedures.

But rights aren’t made real by placing them in a PDF.

They are made real through the allocation of power when something goes wrong. Can the consumer retain money? Can the trader impose sanctions? Who carries the risk while the dispute is being decided? Does the provider have a financial incentive to resolve the problem promptly, or does the student have to spend months pursuing money that has already disappeared into the institution’s accounts?

For home undergraduates, the state-backed payment system removes the student’s direct leverage. For self-funders, university terms often require the leverage to be surrendered before the course has been delivered. For students paying by instalments, debt sanctions may make exercising it practically impossible.

Maybe the persistent gap between the course that was advertised and the experience that is delivered is not only about information, awareness or culture.

Maybe the officer had it right the first time.

They’ve had your money already.

The post What to expect for results day and Clearing 2026: early clues and insights in UCAS data appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
Join HEPI for an ‘In Conversation’ webinar ahead of the 2026 admissions round on 11:00-12:00, 11th August 2026, featuring Dr Jo Saxton CBE, Chief Executive of UCAS. In discussion with Nick Hillman OBE, followed by a live Q&A, the session will explore the key issues shaping this year’s admissions cycle and what they mean for universities, applicants and the wider higher education sector. Register now.

This blog was kindly authored by Maggie Smart, UCAS Director of Data and Analysis and Jo Richards, UCAS Senior Insights Lead.

As attention turns to Qualifications Scotland results day next Tuesday and Level 3 results day the following Thursday, the focus understandably is on what happens when applicants receive their grades. Yet early indicators about this year’s admissions cycle have already emerged.

The 30 June Deadline – the point at which about 96% of prospective students who apply through UCAS have typically submitted their applications – provides a valuable early snapshot of the upcoming university cohort and what could potentially happen in Clearing.

Growing UK 18-year-olds means a growing market

Demand for higher education remains strong this year, with record numbers applying to university and college – highlighting confidence among applicants as we enter the summer results period. Overall, 695,740 students applied by the June deadline this year, compared to 665,070 in 2025. This is up +4.6%.

Looking specifically at UK 18-year-olds, applicant numbers have increased in line with the growth in the population cohort, rising from 328,390 in 2025 to 344,760 in 2026. In turn, the application rate has remained strong and steady, up slightly from 41.2% in 2025 to 41.4% in 2026.

In previous cycles, record numbers of UK 18-year-old applicants have led to record acceptances, and we anticipate more school leavers will be celebrating getting their first (UCAS firm) choice once again this year.

Mature applicants may drive Clearing activity

One applicant group who could have an impact on Clearing this summer is mature learners (aged 21+). Mature applicants are typically more likely than school leavers to apply later in the admissions cycle, including directly to Clearing. By the 30 June deadline this year, 33% of UK mature applicants applied between the January Equal Consideration date (ECD) and 30 June, compared with just 2% of UK 18-year-old applicants.

Although mature applicant demand remains below where it was a decade ago, it has increased by +1% (up from 86,310 to 87,180) compared to June last year, marking the first year-on-year rise in mature applicant numbers at this point in the cycle since 2022.

If the trend of later mature applicants continues, we could certainly see more trying to find an available place directly in Clearing this year.

Offer-making behaviour: balancing demand and capacity

Looking at how providers are responding to applicant demand through their offer-making behaviour also gives a good indication of what we might expect to see on results day.

Overall, universities and colleges have made 2.07m offers to applicants who applied by the January ECD, a +3.2% increase since 2025. While institutions have made more offers this year, this is in response to higher demand and a large proportion of applications have been to higher tariff providers. This has contributed to a small decrease in the overall offer rate, which now stands at 72.6%, down slightly from 72.9% in 2025.

This marginally lower offer rate and the increased number of applicants could potentially lead to more activity in Clearing than last year, among mature and international applicants who have seen slightly lower offer rates across the sector. However, with around 27,000 courses in Clearing, there are plenty of options available for those deciding on their next steps. UCAS research also shows the vast majority of offer holders remain committed to going to university this autumn.

Applicants continue to choose STEM while Social Sciences increases

We are also seeing continued growing demand for particular subject areas, notably across STEM subjects, suggesting applicants are continuing to make informed choices about their future study and employment prospects.

Engineering and Technology has seen the biggest growth in applications by the 30 June deadline, with an increase of +38,260 applications compared to the same point last year (+16.3%). In addition, applications to Mathematical Sciences have also risen, increasing by +11% from 68,150 in 2025 to 75,650 in 2026. However, there has also been a 9.8% increase in applications to Social Sciences, from 317,690 last year to 348,660 this year, while Law has seen an 8.7% uplift, from 176,730 in 2025 to 192,070 this year.

As we look ahead to Clearing, these trends may continue to shape applicant decision making. Every year, we see a wide range of courses available in Clearing across all types of universities and colleges – but the most selective courses at the most selective institutions tend to fill fairly quickly. While we anticipate strong demand for certain subject areas such as STEM in Clearing, students will continue to have a wide range of opportunities available to them – from Maths to Marketing and Medieval Studies.

Cost of living top of the mind for applicants

Financial considerations are increasingly shaping the way students are making decisions about what and where to study, and UCAS research shows cost of living support on offer by universities and colleges is now the third most important consideration for young people exploring their options.

As a result, more applicants are weighing up where to study, where to live and how they’ll cover daily expenses. This may mean more use Decline My Place to apply elsewhere during Clearing – last year, about a third of those placed in Clearing (34%) used DMP. This group of Clearing users typically change their mind to opt for a different choice – a choice that is often closer to home or enables them to live at home.

Among students who were placed through Clearing last year, nearly three quarters (73%) said understanding cost of living at the university or college was important, closely followed by the financial support available (71%) and the cost of travelling between university and home (69%).

Having a realistic understanding of their likely expenses while studying is crucial. Yet new UCAS research this year found fewer than one in three (29%) applicants feel informed about how much money they will need to support themselves at university or college. To help, UCAS has launched a new budget calculator, enabling applicants to estimate living costs across more than 100 UK locations, create a personalised budget, and plan their finances as they consider their options. Students can also use UCAS’ scholarships, bursaries and grants tool to explore the financial support offered by universities and colleges.

With Confirmation and Clearing now on the horizon, we’re keeping an eye on how the 30 June application trends turn into acceptances.

title: College Republicans are fighting and the far right is benefiting: ‘It looks very childish’
summary:
Tensions in the national party are trickling down to US college campuses, where a newer student group is rapidly outflanking longstanding moderate rivals

full_text:
When the Utah county clerk’s office announced last month that it was hiring Kai Schwemmer – an undergraduate at Brigham Young University and a rightwing influencer – to help reach younger voters, an uproar ensued.

An energetic and fast-talking 23-year-old, Schwemmer is a rising star of campus organizing at the College Republicans of America (CRA). He is also a prolific livestreamer with a record of provocation – which returned to haunt him when more than 80 prominent women in Utah signed a letter protesting against his hiring.

Drawing on reporting earlier this year by the Guardian, critics noted that Schwemmer, who had been appointed as chief deputy clerk, had made remarks suggesting women are unsuited to public office, criticizing universal suffrage and endorsing “family voting”, a concept sometimes associated with Christian nationalists. In 2022, he attended a conference organized by Nick Fuentes, an antisemitic far-right pundit, and appeared in a supportive documentary about him.

In March, Schwemmer was also named political director of the CRA, the country’s fastest-growing national federation of college Republicans. When critics raised similar concerns, Martin Bertao, the group’s president, responded: “I would like to apologize… to absolutely NOBODY,” adding that the “CRA will never back down to the WOKE mob!”

The controversies dogging Schwemmer, and the CRA’s cavalier response, are illustrative of the extent to which parts of the college Republican movement – not to be confused with, though also not unlike, the scandal-plagued Young Republicans – have been won over by a hard right that views moderate Republicans with scorn, apes Donald Trump’s confrontational style, and has ties to extremists.

Republican student groups have long acted as a talent pipeline to the national party and helped turn out voters. But ideological, personal and financial disputes in recent years have split the movement into three main national college Republican groups. Since its founding just three years ago, the CRA has grown rapidly, outflanking and displacing two more established – and more moderate – rivals in part thanks to its radical posture.

The CRA is “more ideologically aligned with the next generation of Americans” than other college Republican groups, said Bertao, who is an undergraduate at the University of California, Berkeley.

Each of the three groups views itself as the movement’s true voice – but none are officially recognized by the Republican National Committee.

“As of right now, no one is getting recognition because of this infighting,” said Chaston Atkins, the chair of the Georgia Association of College Republicans, which has made a deliberate choice not to affiliate with any of the national groups. “It looks very childish.”

The factional fighting mirrors tensions in the national party between Reaganite conservatives and those who have embraced Trump’s rightwing populism. At the same time, the sidelining of moderate college Republicans raises questions about the future of a right whose rising leaders tend to be arch-conservative young men, nursed on the far-right internet, who often think that Trump is not radical enough.

The college Republican movement in the United States is more than a century old, and made up of campus clubs that often join state and national federations.

While these clubs and federations hold little political influence in and of themselves, many prominent politicians and activists on the right – including Grover Norquist, Karl Rove, Paul Ryan, Reince Priebus, Roger Stone, Paul Manafort and Kevin McCarthy – had their first taste of power as student politickers in the college Republican movement.

After Charlie Kirk, the far-right organizer and influencer, was killed last year, a groundswell of students rushed to join campus conservative organizations, though the long-term staying power of that groundswell is difficult to gauge.

The organization Kirk founded, Turning Point USA (TPUSA), which is now run by his wife, Erika Kirk, has an overlapping but different niche than traditional college Republican organizations. TPUSA, Atkins said, increasingly caters to previously apolitical young people from conservative Christian backgrounds who wish to see their values better reflected in society, whereas born political animals tend to gravitate to the college Republicans.

When Trump first ran for president, in 2016, many college Republican groups were embarrassed to be too closely associated with a candidate viewed as a loose cannon. As Trump remade the Republican party in his own image, that changed – and the CRA emerged as an upstart ready to most zealously embrace the Maga zeitgeist.

Founded in 2023, the CRA leaped to endorse Trump soon after he announced his 2024 re-election campaign, Bertao said, in contrast to the more center-right National Federation of College Republicans (NFCR), which initially favored Nikki Haley and waited until a month before the general election to endorse Trump.

Bertao also criticized a third group – the country’s oldest, the College Republican National Committee (CRNC) – for having put out a statement urging Americans to respect the verdict when Trump was convicted of fraud in New York.

The NFCR and the CRNC did not respond to queries.

The CRA now claims to represent 350 college chapters nationwide, and continues to grow. Earlier this month it admitted the College Republican Federation of Alabama, which represents six chapters in that state. Its leadership has also increasingly cultivated ties with rightwing nationalist parties in Europe.

Schwemmer told the Guardian that many of his most controversial remarks were made in jest, taken out of context, or interpreted uncharitably. Regarding his attendance at a conference organized by Fuentes, he said: “I’ve been to libertarian conferences and events that leftwing people have put on, and I’ve entirely disagreed with what they’ve had to say.”

This year several local college Republican clubs affiliated with the CRA have gotten into hot water.

In March, a college Republican club at the University of Florida sparked outrage when someone allegedly tied to the club was photographed making a Hitler salute. Soon after, the CRA announced that it was accepting the club as a member.

Earlier that month, the club hosted James Fishback, a long-shot and fiercely anti-Zionist Republican primary candidate for governor who has built a small but dedicated following among college-aged young people with humor that winks at the antisemitism and racism of the online far right.

The CRA and a lawyer representing the club in Florida have said that the person photographed was merely someone who had attended a club event, and held no leadership role.

The same month, a CRA club at Georgetown University wrote on social media that Muslims “have no place in American society. Their religion is incompatible with our Christian Nation.” After a backlash from other campus groups as well as some of its own members, the group deleted the message.

“We affirm the First Amendment rights of all Americans and we are called to love everyone,” a spokesperson for the club at Georgetown told a campus newspaper. “Our properly articulated position is that sharia law is incompatible with Western civilization and American society as it seeks to oppress women and persecute religious minorities.” The CRA told the Guardian that the club’s “actions and sentiment were not wrong; Islam is not compatible with the West”.

And in April, a CRA club at Salisbury University in Maryland invited the writer Jared Taylor to speak with students. Taylor is a self-described “white advocate” whom critics have accused of promoting white supremacy, a label he rejects. According to a New York Times reporter present, Colin McEvers, the college Republican who organized the event with Taylor, introduced him as someone who could help “save our country, to keep it from becoming a non-English-speaking hellscape where white people are spit at, despised and persecuted”.

The CRA said that it did not endorse or sanction the Maryland event. It has also said that “[a]ny sort of bigotry and hatred is wrong and should be widely condemned.”

The CRA also said that it allows individual chapters to “decide on who to bring as speakers because of how different every state and campus is. However, when chapters go away from the main beliefs of our organization, we do intervene and draw clear lines.”

Bertao disputed, in part, the idea that the CRA is more radical than other college Republican organizations. “We don’t necessarily take policy perspective positions,” he said. “We view our role as supporting the Republican party and supporting the administration.”

Yet the CRA’s close mirroring of Trump might come to pose problems for the organization. Recent polling has shown that younger Republican voters are, compared with older ones, less supportive of American intervention abroad, less supportive of Israel, and less in lockstep with Trump.

The CRA’s own website seems to indicate a possible mismatch with a president currently at war with Iran; its mission statement calls for “a conservative movement that prioritizes the needs of the American people … and adheres to non-interventionist policies”.

That dynamic can be seen with Fishback, the Florida candidate for governor; although he trails the Trump-endorsed candidate, Byron Donalds, by a huge margin, polling shows that he is vastly more popular with likely Republican voters aged 18 to 34.

At the same time, survey data does not yield much evidence that younger Republicans, on the whole, hold more radical views than older Republicans on hot-button cultural issues such as abortion or same-sex marriage, Melissa Deckman, the CEO of the Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI), said. She suspects that the radical turn of some college Republicans says more about the views of conservative elites – and aspiring elites on campuses – and their desire to secure influence within the movement.

More hardline views are pushing to the fore, she speculated, as “the activist class within the GOP [struggles] over the direction of their party”.

Asked if the CRA’s membership or mission might conflict with its pro-Trump stance, Schwemmer disagreed: “I think all of us are grateful for the revolution that occurred in conservative politics in 2016, even if we since have disagreed with many of the things the president has done.”

College conservative groups tend to mirror “some of the larger fractiousness on the right”, said Matthew Dallek, a political historian at George Washington University. Historically, insurgent factions periodically emerge to challenge establishments they perceive as having sold out to the political center, displacing them before eventually facing similar rebellions.

Amy Binder, a sociologist at Johns Hopkins who has co-written two books about political organizing on campuses, noted that when she worked on the first – published in 2013 during the Obama administration – she observed two distinct styles of campus conservatism.

Conservatives at smaller, elite schools tended to emphasize the idea of civil discourse and intellectual persuasion and avoid sharp elbows that might rub their peers – and possible fellow future leaders of industry – the wrong way. In contrast, conservatives at big state schools tended to lean into provocation, with stunts such as “affirmative action bake sales” – where baked goods are priced differently according to the buyers’ ethnicity – that might offend people on large, diverse campuses but also impress rightwing political organizations scouting brash young talent.

“They didn’t care if they set off their liberal classmates,” Binder said. “In fact, they thought that was great.” To attract media attention, their attitude was “go big or go home”.

By the time she co-wrote her second book – published in 2022, as the “woke” backlash was gathering steam – the second style had come into its own, and was by far the dominant strain. “Anything that was more civil was really disparaged as being establishment – boring, out of fashion.”

For its part, the Utah county clerk’s office backtracked, partly, in its hiring of Schwemmer; after a furor, the office announced that his job would be adjusted to a more junior role.

Radicalism currently has the upper hand in many quarters, but the future is difficult to predict, noted Atkins, the college Republican in Georgia. Clubs at many schools often have just a handful of members, meaning they may change affiliations quickly because of political winds or the views of a determined faction among the leadership. Similarly, he feels that the CRA has tied itself too closely to the personhood of an unpopular second-term president who will soon diminish in influence.

For those reasons, he cautioned against extrapolating too much from the momentum of the CRA or any other group or faction. “It can change in the blink of an eye,” he said.

title: I’m torn by the hard hat v graduation cap debate. Is it wrong that I want my kids to go to university? | Emma Brockes
summary:
As Andy Burnham intervenes, it’s clear that the shine is coming off higher education. But is society ready for this mindshift? Am I?

For a while now I’ve been having a conversation with friends that a few years ago would’ve been largely unthinkable. Partly, this is because of how sheltered we all tend to be when trying to imagine our kids’ lives running on different tracks to our own. But it’s also about the world changing. A brilliant young person I know left school, took up an internship, turned it into a job and now she’s in her early 20s with no debt and a great position at a big fashion house. “Maybe I won’t go to university, either,” said one of my kids, eyeing me for a reaction, while I nodded thoughtfully and tried to ride out the panic.

Andy Burnham’s announcement this week that university shouldn’t be the single, aspirational goal of all young people is perfectly timed and sensibly presented and shouldn’t sound as radical as it does. It is, of course, a correction to existing norms that university-for-all is a proper national goal and the only personal determinant of ambition and success. By contrast, Burnham said on Tuesday, this country should “value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap” as he spoke about tailoring technical and vocational training to meet local job needs and tackle youth unemployment.
